turn_text: One of the few things that just about everyone in the country can agree on is that America is a very politically divided nation. How can we cool the fiery rhetoric? Former Long Island Democratic Congressman Steve Israel has some ideas on that. He joins us on the record on WCBS. Congressman, good to talk with you again. I do want to touch first on the news of the day. What is your reaction to Joe Biden stepping aside in the presidential race?

Well, it's hard for me to say this because I've always had a close relationship with President Biden, but he did the right thing. He did the right thing for the country. He did the right thing for the Democratic Party. He was overtaken by events, one really horrific evening at the debate, despite his efforts to repair that performance and try and move past it, he just couldn't do it. So he was overtaken by events. I've always said that if election day approaches and it was a referendum on Joe Biden, Democrats would lose. If it's a referendum on Donald Trump, I think Democrats can win. And now this is a referendum on Donald Trump.
Do you expect Vice President Harris to cruise to the nomination, or could we see a floor fight in Chicago next month?

Well, you know, we're Democrats, so we never cruise. So it's going to be some turbulence there, some waves. I will say this, I think Democrats should be advised by history the last time an incumbent Democrat. President made a decision not to seek re-election. It was in 1968 when LBJ made that announcement. That was five months before the convention, and that convention erupted into violence and mayhem and chaos. The party was badly divided, and Richard Nixon then cruised to victory in 1968. That convention was a Chicago, by the way. The Democratic convention is in less than 30 days in Chicago, and we cannot repeat that history. And so I believe it is very important for Democrats to produce a consensus candidate. Nobody should be anointed, but we should develop a consensus. In my view, that consensus should be around Kamala Harris. And then we need a ticket that is going to help unify the party, but importantly, resonate with independent swing moderate centrist voters in the battleground states.

turn_text: Now, you recently co-authored an op-ed in the Hill that suggested that mindfulness and meditation may help to calm our political divisiveness. What do you mean by that?

Yeah, and I know, you know, sometimes it comes across as sounding strange, but there's a real science behind this, and even in military, to a certain extent, has embraced this. When I was in Congress, even before the rise of Donald Trump and the MAGA movement, I noticed that my constituents seemed to be getting more emotional about politics, angrier. My colleagues were getting angrier. The media seemed to be getting angrier. Social media was getting angrier. And I kind of stepped back and tried to understand it. And look, there's no surprise. I mean, you can't even have a family barbecue right now without kind of tiptoeing around politics or being concerned that it's going to become a frothing fight over Donald Trump and Joe Biden or whoever is in our politics. And so a former Congressman Tim Ryan and I began to develop some strategies to deal with that. It's mindfulness, whatever meditation works, it's clearing your brain, clearing the clutter, transcending it, and it's also studying Stoicism. I was a student of philosophy and studied Stoicism which guided George Washington and Abraham Lincoln and guided Dwight D. Eisenhower and should guide us. And so now I'm teaching this with Tim Ryan at Cornell University. We're trying to shape the next generation of leaders with some resilience and a better understanding of how to process and manage political emotions so that we can move towards one another instead of erupting against each other.

turn_text: But isn't asking lawmakers and the public who are so deeply divided to try meditation a little unrealistic?

Well, first of all, it doesn't have to be meditation. It could just be a breeding exercise for a few minutes. And I'll tell you, on this topic of realism, one of the things that so surprised me was we ran into the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Joe Dunford. And he told us that he himself endorsed the practice of mindfulness with his warriors, that chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, one of the toughest Marines I've ever met, tried an experiment. He had one battalion embrace study and practice mindfulness. Another battalion didn't quite embrace it. And what did he say? What did he find? That the battalion of war fighters that was able to clear the clutter from their minds and transcend the emotion at the moment became much more proficient as warriors. They learned that sometimes you don't have to kick in the door. Sometimes you can knock with some force and some assertion and get to the result that you need. So if it works for a bunch of Marines, it should work for anybody. What are the first steps?

turn_text: How do you make this happen?

Well, the first thing you have to do is just look, you can Google, you can go on on the internet and just get some basic information about mindfulness and meditation. And again, it doesn't have to be a long, elaborate practice. The first step is just learning to pause and take a step back. And that's what we did actually with members of Congress. Congressman Ryan formed the Quiet Caucus and trained members not to just go for the jugular, But almost like an Olympic athlete, bomb their movements, take a step back, take that moment, breathe in and find yourself, not go further to the left or the right, but go a little deeper. And then you can take it from there. You can study some meditation techniques. For me, I do meditate. I also read stoicism. And stoicism is all about Dealing with what's in your control and not agonizing over what's out of your control, learning how to manage your egotistical impulses and understanding how to deal with obstacle. It works in C-suites. It works at the highest corporate levels. It works in the military. It needs to work in Congress and in our own lives.
